 Former students set off fireworks in a French classroom amid a wave of violent youth protests over teacher shortages and underfunding in schools.
 Footage filmed at a secondary school in Chelles, east of Paris, shows children fleeing after mortar fireworks were fired towards them. Some students cowered behind desks while others ran into corridors. “It hit my foot,” one cried as bangs rang out and red flashes lit the room.
 Pupils told French television that young people who had “left the school” returned to set off fireworks inside Lycée Jehan-de-Chelles on Monday.
 Several individuals reportedly forced their way into the building, where pupils were ordered to shelter in classrooms. Four pupils suffered minor injuries in the incident. It was the second such intrusion in a month.
 Children were filmed fleeing as fireworks exploded inside the school in Chelles
 It was the latest in a string of violent incidents at schools across France, including a headteacher struck in the head by a paving stone, a politician hit by a bottle filled with petrol, and a classroom set on fire.
 Weeks of school blockades, protests and widespread looting last month prompted calls for tougher policing, with a new survey finding that 85 per cent of French people believe officers are insufficiently protected against rioters.
 Most also back the use of controversial weapons, including stun grenades and rubber-bullet launchers.
 In an editorial, Le Parisien said the most shocking aspect of the Chelles footage was not the fireworks themselves, but that they had occurred “INSIDE a classroom”.
 Widespread looting has prompted calls for tougher policing across France
 Credit : Sameer Al-Doumy /AFP 
 On Tuesday, Angela Pascoa Dos Santos, a councillor and deputy mayor of Chelles, was struck in the chest by a bottle filled with petrol as she helped parents reopen the Lycée Gaston-Bachelard, another secondary school.
 She was uninjured but filed a complaint with police, alleging attempted murder, which has prompted a criminal investigation.
 Emmanuel Macron condemned the attack, saying: “Violence has no place in a democracy.”
 “These acts have nothing to do with expressing grievances,” the French president added. “They amount to brutality and intimidation and must be punished with the utmost severity.”
 Elsewhere, the headteacher of Lycée Émile-Combes in Bègles, near Bordeaux, was rushed to hospital on Monday after being struck on the head by a paving stone.
 In Aix-en-Provence, a classroom at Lycée Émile-Zola was set on fire on Tuesday morning, leaving around 40 other rooms unusable because of smoke damage. Investigators suspect arson, although no direct link to the protests has been established.
 High school students protest over learning conditions in Paris last month
 Credit : Getty/Kiran Ridley
 Édouard Geffray, the education minister, said on Wednesday that 245 education workers had been injured since the protests began in late September.
 “We are facing extraordinary violence in a handful of schools, which has continued to escalate over the past ten days,” he told BFMTV.
 He blamed “organised, radicalised groups”, including outsiders, who were attacking pupils and teachers in classrooms in an attempt to destroy the education system.
 “The first right is the right to attend lessons,” he added, demanding criminal prosecutions while calling on unions, political parties and parents to condemn the attacks unequivocally.
 A wider school protest movement , prompted by demands for more teachers, better buildings and changes to university admissions, appears to be losing steam.
 Only 49 of France’s roughly 3,700 lycées (secondary schools) remained blockaded on Tuesday, according to the education ministry, although student unions have vowed further demonstrations.
 However, public anger at the disorder is growing.
 Gaël Sliman, the head of polling firm Odoxa, said more than 2,200 police officers and gendarmes had been injured since the unrest began – almost twice the 1,233 recorded during the 1968 riots, according to official figures.
 An Odoxa poll for Le Figaro found that 79 per cent of French people believed the government’s handling of the riots was inadequate, while 68 per cent said police lacked sufficient manpower and equipment.
 Students, parents, rights groups and the Left-wing opposition have criticised allegedly heavy-handed policing, with several youths reportedly losing a hand or an eye.
 But far from demanding restraint, 62 per cent of those surveyed backed the use of dispersal grenades, 59 per cent supported stun grenades and 58 per cent backed rubber-bullet launchers.
 Students have complained of rats and cockroaches in classrooms
 Credit : Jean-Francois Badias/AP
 Three-quarters supported deploying soldiers to protect public buildings, while two-thirds favoured immediate police intervention against looters even if it increased the risk of injuries.
 Support for a crackdown extended to social media, with 64 per cent backing temporary bans on platforms in areas affected by the disorder, while 85 per cent favoured tougher punishments for people using social media to organise looting or attacks.
 In an editorial entitled “Everybody loves the police”, Le Figaro contrasted the anti-police chants that are now ubiquitous in protests, with what it called an overwhelming majority standing behind officers.

 L’Union syndicale lycéenne, a student union, condemned the attacks but blamed the government’s failure to address students’ grievances for fuelling tensions.
 Student organisations have called further demonstrations for Saturday and Nov 17, with public-sector workers also expected to take part.
